chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, who said:

I entered upon Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) while I was a youth, so he described voluntary acts and fasting to me. He saw the heaviness of that on my face, so he said to me: 'This is not like the obligatory duty; whoever neglects it is destroyed. Rather, it is voluntary. If you are occupied with it or neglect it, you make it up.'
Indeed, they disliked that their deeds be raised one day complete and one day deficient.
Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Those who are constant at their Prayer.'
And they disliked that they pray until the day declines, for the gates of the sky are opened when the day declines.

key_terms.يَزُولَ النَّهَار: Decline of the day (time for prayer)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between obligatory and voluntary worship in Shia hadith, and how should one handle missed voluntary acts?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) distinguishes voluntary worship from obligatory duties by noting that while neglecting fard leads to ruin, missing nafl is less severe, though scholars disliked leaving any act of worship unperformed for a full day. He emphasizes constancy in prayer, citing the Quranic ideal of those who are constant in their Salah, and links the spiritual significance of the midday decline (Zawal) to the opening of heavenly gates, reflecting the Shia emphasis on maintaining continuous spiritual connection.
